title: Write a Good Excel Prompt
goal: Write prompts that describe your columns, ask for one step at a time and ask for an explanation, then check the reply on your own sheet.

steps.text:
An AI tool can't see your sheet the way you do. It only knows what you tell it, so a vague request gets a vague (or wrong) answer.

• Vague: “Fix my sheet.”
• Clear: “Column C is Qty and column D is Price. In E2, give me one formula for the line total that I can fill down.”

A good prompt does three things:
• **Describes your columns**
• **Asks for one step at a time**
• **Asks for an explanation**, not just the answer

You'll practise each one, and check every reply on the sheet.

steps.prompt:
A prompt names columns by what they **hold** and by letter: “column D is the price per item”.

In this sheet, which column holds the price per item? Click its letter, then press [[Enter]].
steps.wrongFeedback: That's not the price. Read the headers in row 1: **Price** sits in column D.
clues: Order, Status, Qty, Price, Total: count along to Price.

steps.prompt: You want the line total for every order in the sheet above. Which prompt will get the **best** answer?
options: “Column C is Qty, column D is Price. In E2 I want Qty × Price. Give me one formula I can fill down.”
steps.explain: The good prompt names the columns, the target cell and the one job. The AI doesn't have to guess, so you don't have to untangle a wrong guess.
wrongFeedback: “Wrong” how? Which cell? The AI has nothing to work with.
“Sales” could mean a total, a count or a chart. It has to guess your columns too.
clues: Which one says where the data is and what you want back?

steps.prompt:
Finish this prompt: “Column __ is City, column __ is Qty, column __ is Price.”

In ==B6:B8== type the **column letter** for each line, pressing [[Enter]] after each.
steps.explain: B, C and D. With letters **and** what each column holds, the AI can't mix up money and counts. Add units too, like “Price is in ₹” or “Qty is in boxes”.

wrongFeedback.empty: Fill all three cells: one letter each for City, Qty and Price.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Match each line to its header in row 1: City, Qty, Price. One letter per cell.

clues: Look along row 1: A is Order, then count across.

steps.prompt:
Column A holds dates like `03/04/26`. Your team writes **day first**, but your prompt doesn't say so. You ask for “total sales in April”.

What's the risk?
options: None: dates always mean one thing
The AI may read it as 4 March and pick the wrong rows
The AI will refuse to answer
steps.explain: `03/04/26` is 3 April in day-first countries and 4 March in month-first ones, and the AI quietly picks one. Say “dates are dd/mm/yy” in the prompt. Same for units and for numbers stored as text.
wrongFeedback: The same text means two different dates, so the AI has to guess.
It won't refuse. It will guess, which is worse because the answer looks fine.

steps.prompt:
Here's a good prompt: “Column C is Qty, column D is Price. In E2 give the line total, with a **10% discount if Qty is 10 or more**.”

Write the formula the AI should return in ==E2==.
steps.explain: **450.** 10 × 50 = 500, minus 10%. Because the prompt gave the columns and an exact rule, you can check the reply on one row by hand. Row 2 has Qty exactly 10, so it tests the “or more” boundary too.

wrongFeedback.missingFunction: The rule is a decision: if Qty is 10 or more, discount; otherwise don't. That's `IF`.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Row 2 has Qty exactly **10**, and “10 or more” includes it. The total should be 450.

clues: `=IF(test, if yes, if no)`. The test is `C2>=10`.

steps.prompt: You need to tidy city names, remove duplicate customers, total sales by city and draw a chart. What's the **best first message** to an AI?
options: “Do all four and send me the finished file.”
“First only: how do I remove extra spaces from the city names in column B?”
steps.explain: A small step can be checked in seconds, and each reply becomes the starting point for the next. If step 3 goes wrong, you know exactly where.
wrongFeedback: One giant request hides where a mistake crept in, and you can't check four jobs at once.
Too vague: the AI must guess your columns and your goal.
clues: Which message gives you something you can check right away?

steps.prompt: Step 1: “In F2, remove the extra spaces from the city in B2.” The AI replies with one small formula. Write it in ==F2==.
steps.explain: `PUNE`: the spaces are gone, but the capitals are untouched. `TRIM` does only one job, which is exactly why this request was easy to check.

wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Extra spaces are the job of `TRIM`.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: The result should be `PUNE`: spaces removed, capitals left alone.

steps.prompt:
Step 2, a follow-up prompt: “Now make it **Pune**: first letter capital, the rest small.”

Change ==F2== so it does both jobs.
steps.explain: `Pune`. Each follow-up wraps one more function around the last, so you can test every layer. Ask for a bigger formula in one go, and you can't see which part broke.

wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Keep the `TRIM` and wrap `PROPER` around it: both functions must be there.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Aim for `Pune`: no spaces and only the first letter a capital. Put `TRIM` inside `PROPER`.

steps.prompt:
You ask an AI to explain `=IF(C2>=10,C2*D2*0.9,C2*D2)`. It replies:

1. “`C2>=10` checks whether Qty is **more than** 10.”
2. “`C2*D2*0.9` takes 10% off the total.”
3. “Otherwise it returns the plain `C2*D2`.”

Which line is **wrong**?
steps.explain: `>=` means “10 or more”, so Qty of exactly 10 gets the discount too. Ask for “explain each part in one line”, then read it against the formula: AI explanations can be wrong as well.
wrongFeedback: Line 2 is right: ×0.9 keeps 90%, which takes off 10%.
Line 3 is right: when the test fails, `IF` returns the last part.
clues: Which symbol in the formula does line 1 describe?

steps.prompt:
A colleague wrote this prompt: “Column B is Status, column C is Qty, column D is Price. In E2 give the line total, but **0 if the order is Cancelled**.”

Type the formula the AI should return in ==E2==.
steps.explain: **0.** Row 2 is cancelled, so it shouldn't count, even though 3 × 120 = 360. A prompt that names the status column and the exact word gives you a formula you can check at a glance.

wrongFeedback.missingFunction: This is a decision based on the status text: use `IF`.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Row 2 is Cancelled, so its total must be 0, not 360. Test `B2` for the word “Cancelled”.
